claim: Experimental detection of residues critical for protein–protein interactions (PPI) is a time-consuming, costly, and labor-intensive process.
source: Experimental detection of residues critical for protein–protein interactions (PPI) is a time-consuming, costly, and labor-intensive process.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field without specific experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: High-throughput PPI-hot spot prediction methods have been validated using relatively small datasets, which may compromise their predictive reliability.
source: Hence, high-throughput PPI-hot spot prediction methods have been developed, but they have been validated using relatively small datasets, which may compromise their predictive reliability.
evidence: This is a critical assessment stated in the introduction, drawing on general knowledge of the field's limitations.

claim: PPI-hotspotID is a novel method for identifying PPI-hot spots using the free protein structure.
source: Here, we introduce PPI-hotspotID, a novel method for identifying PPI-hot spots using the free protein structure
evidence: This is the main methodological contribution described in the abstract.

claim: PPI-hotspotID was validated on the largest collection of experimentally confirmed PPI-hot spots to date.
source: Here, we introduce PPI-hotspotID, a novel method for identifying PPI-hot spots using the free protein structure, and validated it on the largest collection of experimentally confirmed PPI-hot spots to date.
evidence: The validation is described using the dataset constructed in this study.

claim: PPI-hotspotID yielded better performance than FTMap in detecting PPI-hot spots.
source: PPI-hotspotID yielded better performance than FTMap and SPOTONE, a webserver for predicting PPI-hot spots given the protein sequence.
evidence: This is supported by comparative performance metrics presented in Table 1.

claim: PPI-hotspotID yielded better performance than SPOTONE in detecting PPI-hot spots.
source: PPI-hotspotID yielded better performance than FTMap and SPOTONE, a webserver for predicting PPI-hot spots given the protein sequence.
evidence: This is supported by comparative performance metrics presented in Table 1.

claim: When combined with AlphaFold-Multimer-predicted interface residues, PPI-hotspotID yielded better performance than either method alone.
source: When combined with the AlphaFold-Multimer-predicted interface residues, PPI-hotspotID yielded better performance than either method alone.
evidence: This is supported by performance metrics in Table 2.

source: Furthermore, we experimentally verified several PPI-hotspotID-predicted PPI-hot spots of eukaryotic elongation factor 2.

source: It is available as a web server (https://ppihotspotid.limlab.dnsalias.org/) and open-source code (https://github.com/wrigjz/ppihotspotid/).

evidence: This is a factual statement about resource availability.

claim: Protein–protein interactions (PPIs) play a crucial role in cellular physiology.
source: Protein–protein interactions (PPIs) play a crucial role in cellular physiology, and their dysregulation is associated with various diseases (David et al., 2012) such as cancer (Nero et al., 2014), infectious diseases, and neurodegenerative diseases (Blazer and Neubig, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dysregulation of PPIs is associated with various diseases such as cancer, infectious diseases, and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Protein–protein interactions (PPIs) play a crucial role in cellular physiology, and their dysregulation is associated with various diseases (David et al., 2012) such as cancer (Nero et al., 2014), infectious diseases, and neurodegenerative diseases (Blazer and Neubig, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Identifying residues critical for PPIs is important for elucidating protein function and designing targeted biomedical interventions.
source: Identifying residues critical for PPIs (termed PPI-hot spots) is important for elucidating protein function and designing targeted biomedical interventions (Cukuroglu et al., 2014; Rosell and Fernández-Recio, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PPI-hot spots are conventionally defined as residues whose mutations to alanine cause ≥2 kcal/mol drop in the protein binding free energy.
source: Conventionally, PPI-hot spots are defined as residues whose mutations to alanine cause ≥2 kcal/mol drop in the protein binding free energy (Clackson and Wells, 1995; Bogan and Thorn, 1998; DeLano, 2002; Li et al., 2004; Keskin et al., 2005; Moreira et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a definition supported by multiple citations.

claim: The conventional definition of PPI-hot spots based on alanine mutations limits the number of experimentally determined PPI-hot spots.
source: However, this definition, based on measuring the binding free energy change upon mutation to alanine, limits the number of experimentally determined PPI-hot spots.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of the conventional definition.

claim: PPI-hot spots have been more broadly defined to include residues whose mutations, not necessarily to alanine, significantly impair/disrupt PPIs.
source: Hence, PPI-hot spots have been more broadly defined to include residues whose mutations, not necessarily to alanine, significantly impair/disrupt PPIs (Fischer et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2022), as detected by experimental methods such as coimmunoprecipitation and yeast two-hybrid screening.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: High-throughput PPI-hot spot prediction methods generally fall into two categories: energy-based methods and classifier-based methods.
source: They generally fall into two categories (Rosário‐Ferreira et al., 2022): (1) methods that compute the binding energy/free energy difference between the wild-type protein and a mutant using classical force fields or empirical scoring functions (Moreira et al., 2007; Massova and Kollman, 1999; Huo et al., 2002; Guerois et al., 2002; Kortemme and Baker, 2002; González-Ruiz and Gohlke, 2006; Grosdidier and Fernández-Recio, 2008; Yogurtcu et al., 2008; Barlow et al., 2018; Ibarra et al., 2019). (2) Methods that employ classifiers such as nearest neighbor, support vector machines, decision trees, Bayesian/neural networks, random forest, and ensemble machine-learning models using various features including conservation, secondary structure, solvent-accessible surface area (SASA), and atom density (Rosário‐Ferreira et al., 2022; Darnell et al., 2007; Cho et al., 2009; Assi et al., 2010; Xia et al., 2010; Lise et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2012; Ye et al., 2014; Munteanu et al., 2015; Melo et al., 2016; Moreira et al., 2017; Qiao et al., 2018; Sitani et al., 2021; Ovek et al., 2022).
evidence: This categorization is supported by extensive citations to prior literature.

claim: Most PPI-hot spot prediction methods rely on the protein complex structure.
source: Most of the PPI-hot spot prediction methods rely on the protein complex structure and some are accessible via webservers; for example, Hotpoint (Tuncbag et al., 2010), KFC2 (Zhu and Mitchell, 2011), PredHS (Deng et al., 2014), and PredHS2 (Wang et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific methods.

claim: Fewer PPI-hot spot prediction methods use only the free protein structure or sequence.
source: Fewer methods use only the free protein structure (Higa and Tozzi, 2009; Zerbe et al., 2012; Ozbek et al., 2013; Agrawal et al., 2014; Kozakov et al., 2015) or sequence (Qiao et al., 2018; Ofran and Rost, 2007; Chen et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2013; Huang and Zhang, 2016; Hu et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2018; Preto and Moreira, 2020; Yao et al., 2022), and SPOTONE (hot SPOTs ON protein complexes with Extremely randomized trees) is available as a web server.
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific methods.

claim: SPOTONE predicts PPI-hot spots from the protein sequence using residue-specific features.
source: SPOTONE (Preto and Moreira, 2020) predicts PPI-hot spots from the protein sequence using residue-specific features such as atom type, amino acid (aa) properties, secondary structure propensity, and mass-associated values to train an ensemble of extremely randomized trees.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the SPOTONE paper.

claim: PPI-hot spot prediction methods have mostly been trained, validated, and tested on data from ASEdb and/or SKEMPI 2.0 database.
source: The PPI-hot spot prediction methods have mostly been trained, validated, and tested on data from the Alanine Scanning Energetics database (ASEdb) (Thorn and Bogan, 2001) and/or the Structural Kinetic and Energetic database of Mutant Protein Interactions (SKEMPI) 2.0 database (Jankauskaite et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the databases.

claim: Antibody–antigen interactions have different sequence and structural characteristics compared to non-antibody PPIs.
source: However, antibody–antigen interactions have different sequence and structural characteristics compared to non-antibody PPIs (Wang et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The focus of this study is exclusively on non-antibody proteins.
source: Therefore, our focus is exclusively on non-antibody proteins in this study.

evidence: This is a factual statement about the database content.

claim: ASEdb and SKEMPI together contain 399 distinct PPI-hot spots in 132 proteins.
source: Altogether, ASEdb and SKEMPI contain 399 distinct PPI-hot spots in 132 proteins.

source: The proteins in PPI-Hotspot+PDBBM share <60% sequence identity, which has been shown to be a reasonable threshold for grouping domains with similar functions (Chen et al., 2022).

source: Using this dataset, we applied an automatic machine-learning framework that automates the machine-learning pipeline to detect PPI-hot spots using the aa type as well as structural, energetic, and evolutionary features of each residue in a protein.
evidence: This is described in the Materials and methods section and used throughout the Results.

claim: PPI-hotspotID identifies PPI-hot spots using an ensemble of classifiers and only four residue features: conservation, aa type, SASA, and gas-phase energy.
source: The resulting prediction model, named PPI-hotspotID, identifies PPI-hot spots using an ensemble of classifiers and only four residue features (conservation, aa type, SASA, and gas-phase energy, ΔGgas).

claim: PPI-hotspotID correctly predicted all four experimentally known GCP60 PPI-hot spots including F19 and Y46, which do not form hydrogen bonds across the interface with PI4K-β.
source: An illustrative example is the binding of Golgi resident protein (GCP60) with phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase β (PI4K-β). PPI-hotspotID correctly predicted all four experimentally known GCP60 PPI-hot spots including F19 and Y46, which do not form hydrogen bonds across the interface with PI4K-β (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: F19 in GCP60 is in vdW contact with Q42, which in turn forms vdW contacts with H45.
source: Although F19 and Y46 do not directly contact PI4K-β, F19 is in van der Waals (vdW) contact with Q42, which in turn forms vdW contacts with H45, whereas Y46 is in vdW contact with both H45 and Y49.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: Y46 in GCP60 is in vdW contact with both H45 and Y49.
source: Although F19 and Y46 do not directly contact PI4K-β, F19 is in van der Waals (vdW) contact with Q42, which in turn forms vdW contacts with H45, whereas Y46 is in vdW contact with both H45 and Y49.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3.

claim: Proteins typically interact with multiple partners, but their PPI-hot spots may have been experimentally characterized for only a few partners.
source: Proteins typically interact with multiple partners, but their PPI-hot spots may have been experimentally characterized for only a few partners.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation.

claim: Some PPI-hotspotID-predicted residues might be potential PPI-hot spots for other binding partners.
source: In some cases where PPI-hotspotID predicted residues that were absent in the PPI-Hotspot+PDBBM(1.1) as PPI-hot spots, the protein's complex structures with other binding partners show intermolecular hydrogen bonds between PPI-hotspotID-predicted residues and residues of the respective partner proteins. This suggests that some of the PPI-hotspotID-predicted residues might be potential PPI-hot spots for other binding partners.
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of complex structures with different partners.

claim: The death domain of CRADD contains 7 experimentally known PPI-hot spots (N121, Q125, Y146, R147, K149, V156, Q169) critical for its interaction with PIDD.
source: For example, the death domain of CRADD (caspase-recruitment domain and death domain-containing adaptor protein) contains 7 experimentally known PPI-hot spots (N121, Q125, Y146, R147, K149, V156, Q169) critical for its interaction with PIDD (p53-induced death domain-containing protein).
evidence: This is based on experimental data.

claim: Based on the free crystal structure of CRADD, PPI-hotspotID correctly predicted three true positives (Y146, R147, and Q169), as well as G128.
source: Based on the free crystal structure of CRADD (PDB 2O71-A) (Park and Wu, 2006), PPI-hotspotID correctly predicted three true positives (Y146, R147, and Q169), as well as G128.
evidence: This is based on PPI-hotspotID predictions.

claim: In the oligomeric structure of CRADD-PIDD, G128 shows no hydrogen-bonding interactions, but its neighbor, L127, forms a backbone – side chain hydrogen bond with R147 in another CRADD chain.
source: In the oligomeric structure (PDB 2OF5) (Park et al., 2007) of seven CRADD proteins in complex with five PIDD proteins, G128 shows no hydrogen-bonding interactions, but its neighbor, L127, forms a backbone – side chain hydrogen bond with R147 in another CRADD chain (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: A positively charged G128R mutation would repel the nearby positively charged R147 in another CRADD chain, thus disrupting the CRADD–CRADD interface and decreasing CRADD's affinity for PIDD.
source: A positively charged G128R mutation would repel the nearby positively charged R147 in another CRADD chain, thus disrupting the CRADD–CRADD interface and decreasing CRADD's affinity for PIDD.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on structural analysis.

claim: Experimental data showed that the G128R CRADD mutant did not co-immunoprecipitate the PIDD death domain.
source: Experimental data showed that the G128R CRADD mutant did not co-immunoprecipitate the PIDD death domain, and patients who have non-syndromic mental retardation possess the G128R mutant (Puffenberger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Patients who have non-syndromic mental retardation possess the G128R CRADD mutant.
source: Experimental data showed that the G128R CRADD mutant did not co-immunoprecipitate the PIDD death domain, and patients who have non-syndromic mental retardation possess the G128R mutant (Puffenberger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: PPI-hotspotID could unveil a PPI-hot spot, G128, that is not apparent from the 2OF5 complex structure.
source: Thus, PPI-hotspotID could unveil a PPI-hot spot, G128, that is not apparent from the 2OF5 complex structure: although G128 does not directly interact with PIDD, its mutation, especially to an Arg, might perturb the CRADD–CRADD interface and thus CRADD's oligomeric structure and binding affinity for PIDD.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and experimental analysis.

claim: Alanine-scanning mutagenesis and protein–protein complex structure determination to identify PPI-hot spots are laborious, time-consuming, and costly.
source: The ability of PPI-hotspotID to detect PPI-hot spots provides biologists with a useful tool, as alanine-scanning mutagenesis and protein–protein complex structure determination to identify PPI-hot spots are laborious, time-consuming, and costly.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Conventional methods based on complex structures might miss nonobvious PPI-hot spots with no direct interactions with the protein's partner.
source: Conventional methods based on complex structures might miss nonobvious PPI-hot spots with no direct interactions with the protein's partner.
evidence: This is inferred from the limitations of complex structure-based methods.

claim: AlphaFold-Multimer and future improved protein–protein complex prediction methods require knowledge of interacting partners and independent calculations for each known partner, which reduces the overall efficiency.
source: AlphaFold-Multimer and future improved protein–protein complex prediction methods require knowledge of interacting partners and independent calculations for each known partner, which reduces the overall efficiency.
evidence: This is a limitation stated based on the nature of these methods.

claim: Solved/modeled protein–protein complex structures only reveal the interface residues.
source: Moreover, solved/modeled protein–protein complex structures only reveal the interface residues.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of complex structures.

claim: PPI-hotspotID can reveal nonobvious PPI-hot spots as well as potential PPI-hot spots for other protein partners, thus helping to elucidate the different PPI mechanisms.
source: In contrast, PPI-hotspotID can reveal nonobvious PPI-hot spots as well as potential PPI-hot spots for other protein partners, thus helping to elucidate the different PPI mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of PPI-hotspotID.

claim: The updated benchmark PPI-Hotspot+PDBBM(1.1) contains 414 PPI-hot spots.
source: The updated benchmark, termed PPI-Hotspot+PDBBM(1.1), contains 414 PPI-hot spots.
evidence: This is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Among the 414 PPI-hot spots in PPI-Hotspot+PDBBM(1.1), 104 PPI-hot spots in 32 nonredundant proteins are based on mutations resulting in ΔΔGbind ≥ 2 kcal/mol from ASEdb and SKEMPI2.0 with no known mutations resulting in ΔΔGbind < 0.5 kcal/mol.
source: Among these, 104 PPI-hot spots in 32 nonredundant proteins are based on mutations resulting in ΔΔGbind ≥ 2 kcal/mol from ASEdb (Thorn and Bogan, 2001) and SKEMPI2.0 (Jankauskaite et al., 2019) with no known mutations resulting in ΔΔGbind < 0.5 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The remaining 310 PPI-hot spots in 128 nonredundant proteins are based on mutations that are manually curated in UniProtKB to significantly impair/disrupt PPIs.
source: The remaining 310 PPI-hot spots in 128 nonredundant proteins are based on mutations that are manually curated in UniProtKB (UniProt Consortium, 2018) to significantly impair/disrupt PPIs.
evidence: This is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Two of the proteins have PPI-hot spots from ASEdb/SKEMPI2.0 and UniProtKB, resulting in a total of 158 nonredundant proteins with free structures harboring 414 PPI-hot spots.
source: Two of the proteins have PPI-hot spots from ASEdb/SKEMPI2.0 and UniProtKB, resulting in a total of 158 nonredundant proteins with free structures harboring 414 PPI-hot spots.
evidence: This is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The four most important residue features for PPI-hotspotID are conservation (kC), aa residue type, SASA, and gas-phase energy (ΔGgas).
source: The importance test results revealed the four most important residue features, which in order of their importance are (i) kC, (ii) aa residue type, (iii) SASAi, and (iv) ΔGigas.
evidence: This is based on feature importance analysis.

claim: These four features were used to train an ensemble of machine-learning models using the entire dataset, consisting of 414 true PPI-hot spots and 504 nonhot spots.
source: These four features were used to train an ensemble of machine-learning models using the entire dataset, consisting of 414 true PPI-hot spots and 504 nonhot spots.
evidence: This is described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The resulting PPI-hot spot prediction model yielded an F1 score comparable to the F1 score obtained using the initial set of 10 features.
source: The resulting PPI-hot spot prediction model, named PPI-hotspotID, yielded an F1 score comparable to the F1 score obtained using the initial set of 10 features.
evidence: This is based on model performance comparison.

claim: Calculations for a 539-residue protein (PDB 1c2bA) using PPI-hotspotID took 35 min.
source: Calculations for a 539-residue protein (PDB 1c2bA) took 35 min.
evidence: This is a performance metric for the web server.

claim: Binding of CPEB2 to eEF2 may interfere with conformational changes of eEF2 on ribosomes, thereby affecting the efficiency of eEF2-mediated GTP hydrolysis, and slowing down translation of HIF-1α mRNA.
source: Binding of cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding protein-2 (CPEB2) to eEF2 may interfere with conformational changes of eEF2 on ribosomes, thereby affecting the efficiency of eEF2-mediated GTP hydrolysis, and slowing down translation of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)–1α mRNA (Chen and Huang, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Mouse eEF2 shares 99% sequence identity with human eEF2.
source: To validate PPI-hotspotID's predictions, we mutated the aforementioned predicted PPI-hot spots and PPI-nonhot spots in mouse eEF2 (meEF2), which shares 99% sequence identity with human eEF2.
evidence: This is stated as a fact.

claim: The 414 true PPI-hot spots represent only 2% of the total number of residues (21,722) in the 158 proteins.
source: Note that the 414 true PPI-hot spots represent only 2% of the total number of residues (21,722) in the 158 proteins.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the dataset.
